case.label: D
case.text: Allowing all traffic in both directions also restores every customer connection and removes any doubt about which ephemeral range each client operating system uses; it fails only on the MOST secure qualifier, because it opens every port inbound, which the narrower outbound ephemeral rule does not.

case.label: D
case.text: An interface endpoint for Amazon S3 also keeps the uploads private and off the NAT gateway, and leaves the NAT path for software updates; it loses only on cost, because it adds hourly and per-GB endpoint charges for several terabytes a night, while the gateway endpoint has no such charges.

case.label: B
case.text: A candidate who remembers that a custom network ACL denies everything could add an inbound HTTPS rule; but the stem says the subnet uses the default network ACL, which allows all inbound and outbound traffic, so the only missing piece is the 0.0.0.0/0 route to the internet gateway in the new subnet's route table.

case.label: A
case.text: A new /16 VPC is the cleaner long-term design for 'the next stage of growth' and avoids future limits on how many secondary CIDR blocks one VPC can hold; it loses only on LEAST operational overhead, because a migration and VPC deletion is far more work than adding a secondary CIDR and new subnets in place.

case.label: C
case.text: Public subnets with tight security groups can block all inbound internet traffic to the application and database instances; but the stem requires no direct network path to or from the internet, and a public subnet with a route to the internet gateway is such a path, so only private subnets meet it.

case.label: B
case.text: A rule for the CIDR blocks of the two application subnets also survives changing instance IP addresses with no script; it is less secure only because any other resource launched in those subnets could reach port 3306, while a security group reference admits only members of the application tier.

case.label: D
case.text: An Auto Scaling group of NAT instances with AMI replacement automates recovery and patching to some degree; it still leaves the team owning the instances, the failover routing and the per-instance bandwidth ceiling, which a managed NAT gateway removes.

case.label: B
case.text: Allowing all outbound traffic from the service subnet also fixes the rejected responses, and the stem never states what the service subnet ACL holds today; it loses only on MOST secure, and the Amazon Linux client detail is a strong wording cue that points to the 32768-61000 range in the narrower rule.

case.label: D
case.text: Proxy instances in a public subnet also let the private instances reach IPv6 update servers while the internet cannot open connections to the private instances; they lose on LEAST operational overhead, because the egress-only internet gateway is managed and needs only one ::/0 route.

case.label: C
case.text: Older study material says an Elastic IP address is free while it is associated with a running instance, which would make option C a zero-cost fix; current AWS pricing bills every public IPv4 address, in use or not, so C does not reduce the charge and B is the only option that removes 400 addresses.

case.label: A
case.text: A 0.0.0.0/0 route to the internet gateway makes the existing Elastic IP addresses work at once, and security groups still block unsolicited inbound traffic; it is less secure only because it gives each instance a direct inbound path from the internet, which a NAT gateway in the public subnet does not.

case.label: D
case.text: Referencing the load balancer security group stops the malicious range from hitting the instances' public IP addresses directly, which is part of 'reaching the application'; but requests from that range still pass through the load balancer, so only a network ACL deny rule, which also covers the instances that share those subnets, blocks every request.

case.label: B
case.text: A candidate who thinks of subnets like VPCs could believe a subnet can be extended into a second Availability Zone; a subnet lives in exactly one zone, so a new subnet in the second zone behind the already two-zone load balancer is the fix.

case.label: D
case.text: An interface endpoint also keeps the S3 uploads off the internet gateway while the 0.0.0.0/0 route stays for the partner website; it loses on LEAST operational overhead because it needs an application change to the endpoint DNS name, while the gateway endpoint works through the more specific prefix-list route with no code change.

case.label: C
case.text: VPC Flow Logs are the usual answer for 'monitor network traffic' and can be queried with Athena; but they record metadata about connections, not packet payloads, so they cannot meet the full-content inspection requirement that Traffic Mirroring to the UDP Network Load Balancer meets.

case.label: B
case.text: A gateway endpoint is the cheaper and simpler S3 endpoint inside a VPC, and the option's wording about the subnets that Direct Connect traffic enters makes it look like it applies; but a gateway endpoint is reached only through VPC route tables and cannot be used from an on-premises network, so the interface endpoint is needed.

case.label: D
case.text: A standby NAT gateway in each zone looks like extra protection for high availability; it only adds cost, because a NAT gateway is already redundant within its zone, and one NAT gateway per zone with zone-local routes meets the requirement.

case.label: E
case.text: Interface endpoints for S3 in each zone also remove S3 traffic from the NAT gateway and keep it zone-local, cutting both named charges for that traffic; they lose on MOST cost-effective because they add hourly and per-GB charges, while the gateway endpoint has none.

case.label: D
case.text: A regional NAT gateway in manual mode also removes the public subnets and per-zone routes and gives full control of which zones are served; it loses on LEAST operational overhead because someone must add and remove zones as the Auto Scaling groups move, which automatic mode does on its own.

case.label: E
case.text: A NAT gateway in every zone of the Region gives the most room for later growth into more zones; it fails MOST cost-effective because it pays for NAT gateways in zones that have no workers, while one extra NAT gateway in the second zone covers the failure of the first zone.

case.label: A
case.text: The stem spends a sentence on the malicious IP range, which pulls toward the network ACL deny rule; but the stated requirement is that only the load balancer may reach the instances, which a deny rule for one range does not achieve and a security group reference to the load balancer does.

case.label: C
case.text: A second NAT gateway with zone-local routes also removes cross-zone data transfer charges, which could lower the bill if the update traffic were large; the stem says the updates are small and a zone outage is acceptable, so the added hourly NAT gateway charge makes keeping the current design the cheaper choice.
